transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I spend most of the day checking things in the house over and over—outlets, locks, tools, even dust. I keep going back and fixing or checking them again until I’m exhausted, but I still don’t feel sure enough to leave them alone.
When you start checking, is it because an unwanted thought keeps coming into your mind that something might be wrong?

Yeah. Even when I know I did something right, these awful thoughts pop in that maybe I missed a loose wire and the house could burn down, or left a nail somewhere that could hurt my wife. I try to push the thoughts away, but they just come back stronger.
When you check things, do you feel you have to do it in a particular way or repeat it until it feels just right?

Yes. I keep going back over the outlets, locks, tools—everything—and checking or fixing it again and again. I don’t feel like I can leave it alone until I’m completely worn out, and even then I’m still not sure it’s okay.
When you check things, does it temporarily relieve the anxiety from those thoughts?

It helps for a little while, I guess, but then I start worrying again and go back to check the same things. I can spend most of the day doing it—outlets, locks, tools, even dust—until I’m worn out, and I still don’t feel sure enough to stop.
Do you feel that all this checking is excessive or unreasonable?

Yeah, I know it’s a lot. I spend most of the day going over the outlets, locks, tools, even dust, checking and fixing things again. But I still don’t feel sure enough to just leave it alone, even when I’m completely worn out.
Before you start checking, do the fears about causing harm—like a fire or your wife getting hurt—pop into your mind against your will?

Yes. Even when I know I did something right, these awful thoughts just jump in—like I missed a loose wire and the house will burn down, or I left a nail somewhere and it’ll hurt my wife. I try to push them away, but they just come back stronger.
If you tried to resist checking, would the anxiety become very strong?

Yes. If I try not to check, it builds up really fast. I end up going back over the outlets, locks, tools, even the dust, again and again until I’m exhausted, but I still can’t feel sure enough to leave it alone.
Apart from the checking itself, do unwanted thoughts keep coming back into your mind even when you are not checking?

Yes. Even when I’m not checking, I’ll think I missed a loose wire and the house is going to burn down, or that I left a nail somewhere that could hurt my wife. I know I did the job right, but the thoughts keep coming back. I try to push them out, and it just seems to make them stronger.
Which troubles you more: the unwanted thoughts, or the checking?

The checking, I think. I spend most of the day going back over the outlets, locks, tools, even the dust—checking and fixing things again and again. By the end I’m worn out, and I still don’t feel sure enough to stop.
Are the unwanted thoughts themselves very distressing to you, even before you start checking?

Yes, they are. Even before I start checking, I get really upset thinking I might have missed a loose wire and the house could burn down, or left a nail that could hurt my wife. I know I did the job right, but the thoughts just jump back in. Trying to push them away makes them come back even stronger.
Would you say the unwanted thoughts and the checking bother you about equally?

No, the checking bothers me more. I spend most of the day going back over the outlets, locks, tools, even the dust, fixing or checking them again and again. It wears me out, and I still don’t feel sure enough to just leave it alone.
Would you say the checking rituals are the main problem for you, more than the intrusive thoughts themselves?

Yes. The checking is the main thing. I keep going back over the outlets, locks, tools, even the dust, fixing or checking them again and again. It takes up most of my day, and I’m exhausted, but I still don’t feel sure enough to leave it alone.
